I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

I can't deal with even the slightest upset
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

vignette: Kofi's eyes still widened when he recalled the night he was assaulted outside a bar in his neighborhood. It had been a warm summer evening, and he had just left a friend's birthday celebration to grab some fresh air. As he walked down the street, a group of strangers approached him, their faces twisted in anger. One of them threw a bottle that shattered on the sidewalk beside Kofi's feet, and he remembered feeling like time slowed as they closed in around him. He tried to defend himself, but there were too many of them. The next thing he knew, he was lying on the ground, his head throbbing. The memories of that night still came to Kofi in snapshots – a few disjointed moments frozen in his mind like photographs. When they returned, as they often did, he felt overwhelmed by emotion and had to stop whatever he was doing. He couldn't find the words to describe what had happened, even when he tried to talk about it with friends or family. They would ask him questions, but Kofi just shook his head, feeling like he was drowning in a sea of feelings. As an urban planner, Kofi was used to navigating crowded streets and noisy environments, but since the assault, every sudden sound made him jump – car horns, slamming doors, even the rustling of leaves. He had come to believe that he couldn't trust his own safety, no matter where he was or who was with him. Even when friends reassured him that everything would be okay, Kofi just couldn't shake off the feeling of vulnerability. Kofi's colleagues at work began to notice changes in him too. He avoided meetings and team discussions, fearing conflict or disagreement. If someone raised their voice, even in a calm conversation, Kofi would flinch and quickly excuse himself. The smell of alcohol, which had once been a familiar scent from social gatherings, now made his stomach turn. To cope with these feelings, Kofi turned to self-blame rumination. He dwelled on what he thought he had done wrong that night – if only he had stayed inside the bar, if only he had walked faster – and wondered why he couldn't defend himself better. This line of thinking only made him feel more helpless, like he was trapped in a never-ending cycle of self-doubt. Kofi also started gambling online to distract himself from his emotions. He would spend hours playing games or betting on sports, trying to recapture the thrill and excitement that had been missing from his life since the assault. But even this temporary escape wasn't enough to quiet the voice in his head that kept telling him he was a failure. Six months after the assault, Kofi realized he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this – constantly on edge, unable to trust anyone or anything. The final straw came when he snapped at a colleague who had simply asked him for feedback on a project. The look of shock and concern on her face made Kofi realize how far he had fallen. As he sat in his therapist's office, Kofi felt like he was drowning all over again – this time, not just from memories but from the weight of his own fears and doubts. What frightened him most was that he might never be able to shake off these feelings, that he would be trapped forever in this state of hypervigilance and self-blame. But with a hesitant voice, Kofi began to share his story, hoping against hope that someone could help him rebuild the life he had lost.
